challenges.name: inbox-dedup-quiz
challenges.title: Is the duplicate skipped, counted or lost?
challenges.description: Two consumers of certificate.issued: one that deduplicates in Redis before writing to PostgreSQL, and one with an inbox table hit by two sessions at once.

questions.explanation: False. The key was written by SET NX before the UPDATE, and Redis does not know whether the UPDATE or the ack ever happened. consumer-3 finds seen:m-4410, takes the 'already processed' branch and acks: the certificate is never counted. The deduplication record and the effect live in two different stores, so they cannot commit together; moving the SET after the UPDATE only flips the failure into a double count. The fix is to record the message id in the same PostgreSQL transaction as the UPDATE. The misconception is that a fast dedup cache in front of the database is atomic with the database write.

True. A unique index makes a second insert of the same key wait for the transaction that inserted it first. If that transaction commits, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING inserts nothing and reports 0 rows; if it rolls back, the second insert goes through. So the row count of the inbox insert is the answer to 'did someone else already process this message?', and it is correct even when two consumers race. The handler skips the effect, commits and acks. The misconception is that a check-then-insert (SELECT, then INSERT) is equivalent: two sessions can both see 'not found' and both apply the effect.

challenges.name: inbox-dedup-certificate-counters
challenges.title: An inbox for the certificate counters
challenges.description:
The CodeDev course dashboard shows how many certificates each course has issued. The certificates service publishes `certificate.issued` events (payload `{ courseId, userId }`) and the broker delivers at least once: a message that was not acked, because the consumer crashed, is delivered again. The counters drifted above the real number of certificates. Write `InboxConsumer` so that every message changes the counters at most once while its id is remembered.

`handle(msg, now)` returns "processed", "duplicate" or "invalid":
- "invalid" when `msg.id` or `msg.payload.courseId` is not a non-empty string: change nothing;
- "duplicate" when the inbox already has a row for `msg.id`: change nothing;
- "processed" otherwise: in ONE `db.tx`, insert the inbox row (`msg.id` -> `{ processedAt: now }`) and add 1 to `counters[courseId]` (a missing counter counts as 0). The check belongs in the same transaction.

`cleanup(now, retentionMs)` deletes, in one `db.tx`, every inbox row with `now - processedAt >= retentionMs` and returns how many rows it deleted. The inbox only remembers ids inside the retention window: a message delivered again after its row was deleted is processed again. That is the documented limit of this design.

The tests crash the process just before or just after the commit of the transaction that changes the counters. After a crash the runner starts a new `InboxConsumer` on the same database: anything kept in the consumer object is lost. Never catch `Crash`.

Input (JSON): a list of steps: `{ "deliver": { "id", "courseId", "userId" }, "crash"?: "beforeCommit" | "afterCommit" }`, `{ "advance": ms }` (fake clock), `{ "cleanup": retentionMs }`.

Output (printed by the runner): one line per delivery (`t=<now> <id> <course>: processed, acked` / `duplicate, acked` / `invalid, acked` / `crashed before commit, not acked` / `crashed after commit, not acked`), one line per cleanup (`cleanup removed N`), then `counters: <course>=<n> ...` and `inbox: <n> rows`.
hints: The process dies right after the counter commit and before the ack, and the same message comes back to a brand-new consumer object. What survived the crash that can tell the new consumer it has already counted this id?

Look at where handle reads the inbox and where it writes the counter: the check, the inbox row and the counter must all happen inside the same db.tx callback. In cleanup, look at the comparison with retentionMs for a row that is exactly retentionMs old.

A similar consumer counts lessons done per user. Delivery l7 at t=0 commits { inbox l7, lessonsDone[u4] + 1 } in one transaction, then crashes before the ack; the redelivery finds l7 in the inbox and returns duplicate. With a retention of 1000 ms, cleanup at t=1000 deletes l7 (1000 - 0 >= 1000), so a delivery of l7 at t=1500 is counted again.

tests.name: Three certificates in two courses are each counted once
tests.expected:
t=0 m1 sql-101: processed, acked
t=0 m2 react-201: processed, acked
t=1000 m3 sql-101: processed, acked
counters: react-201=1 sql-101=2
inbox: 3 rows

tests.name: A message delivered twice is counted once
tests.expected:
t=0 m1 sql-101: processed, acked
t=5000 m1 sql-101: duplicate, acked
t=5000 m2 sql-101: processed, acked
counters: sql-101=2
inbox: 2 rows

tests.name: Crash after commit, before ack: the redelivery after restart is a duplicate
tests.expected:
t=0 m1 sql-101: crashed after commit, not acked
t=30000 m1 sql-101: duplicate, acked
t=30000 m2 react-201: processed, acked
counters: react-201=1 sql-101=1
inbox: 2 rows

tests.name: Crash before commit: nothing is saved and the redelivery is processed
tests.expected:
t=0 m1 sql-101: crashed before commit, not acked
t=30000 m2 sql-101: processed, acked
t=30000 m1 sql-101: processed, acked
counters: sql-101=2
inbox: 2 rows

tests.name: Cleanup at the retention boundary; a duplicate after its row was deleted counts again
tests.expected:
t=0 m1 sql-101: processed, acked
t=3600000 m2 react-201: processed, acked
t=86400000 cleanup removed 1
t=86400000 m2 react-201: duplicate, acked
t=86400000 m1 sql-101: processed, acked
t=172800000 cleanup removed 2
counters: react-201=1 sql-101=2
inbox: 0 rows

tests.name: Invalid messages (no id, empty course) change nothing and are acked
tests.expected:
t=0 (no id) sql-101: invalid, acked
t=0 (no id) sql-101: invalid, acked
t=0 m9 (no course): invalid, acked
t=0 m1 sql-101: processed, acked
counters: sql-101=1
inbox: 1 rows
